title: Adams and Jefferson Begin Writing Again
text:
John Adams and Thomas Jefferson had worked side by side in the American Revolution and as diplomats in Europe, and they had become close friends. Party politics in the 1790s drove them apart. In the bitter election of 1800 Jefferson defeated Adams for the presidency, and Adams left Washington early on the morning of Jefferson's inauguration. For more than ten years the two men did not write to each other.

Their mutual friend Benjamin Rush, the Philadelphia physician, worked patiently to bring them together. He wrote to each of them, urging reconciliation, and even told Adams of a dream in which the two old friends renewed their correspondence.

On January 1, 1812, Adams sent Jefferson a short, friendly letter. Jefferson answered warmly. Over the next fourteen years they exchanged well over a hundred letters about politics, religion, books, old age and the meaning of the Revolution.

Both men died on the same day, July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Adams's last words were reportedly that Jefferson still survived. Jefferson had died a few hours earlier.
lesson: A friendship broken by a quarrel can often be saved by a patient go-between and one short first letter. Someone has to write it.
people: John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Rush
location: Quincy, Massachusetts, and Monticello, Virginia, USA
source: Lester J. Cappon, ed., The Adams-Jefferson Letters (1959)
caveat: Adams's last words come from family recollection and are not certain.
